title: STAR 1 check: structure and strong answers

items.q: In a 90-second STAR answer, which part should take the most time?
choices: Situation
Task
Action
Result
items.why: The Action is what the interviewer is scoring: your reasoning, your tools, your decisions. Aim for about half the answer. Long Situations are the most common way candidates run out of time.

choices: "And then it worked."
"The machine was fixed and everyone was happy."
"The trips stopped. It didn't recur in the 3 months I tracked it, and I added the check to the monthly PM."
"We fixed it."
items.why: It has a measurable outcome (no recurrence over a stated period) and a prevention step. The others don't tell the interviewer how you know it was fixed or what you changed.

items.q: Which Action sentence shows structured diagnosis best?
choices: "I tried a few things until it worked."
"I replaced the sensor, then the cable, then the input card."
"I measured 24 V at the terminal block but 0 V at the sensor connector, which ruled out the power supply and pointed to the cable run."
"I used my experience to figure it out."
items.why: It names a measurement, what it showed, what it ruled out, and the next step. That's hypothesis testing. The second option is a parts cannon: it may fix the problem but it doesn't show diagnosis.

items.q: You don't remember the exact downtime. What should you say?
choices: Make up a precise number; it sounds more professional
Give an honest estimate marked as one, such as "about 30 to 45 minutes per stop"
Leave the result out entirely
Say "a lot of downtime"
items.why: An honest, marked estimate is credible and defensible. A made-up precise number collapses under a follow-up question, and once one number is doubted, the whole story is.

items.q: Your supervisor ordered the replacement part and you did the diagnosis and repair. Which phrasing is right?
choices: "I ordered the part and fixed it."
"We fixed it."
"I traced it to the drive's encoder cable; my supervisor approved and ordered the part, and I replaced it and verified it over the next shift."
Leave the supervisor out so the story is about you
items.why: It claims exactly what you did, credits the other person precisely, and still makes your role clear. "We" hides your contribution; claiming the order is inaccurate.

items.q: Your story is full of PLC addresses and part numbers, and the interviewer is a software engineer. Best fix?
choices: Keep it: jargon proves expertise
Name the tool, then say in plain words what it told you; go deeper only if asked
Remove all technical content
Switch to a non-technical story
items.why: Interviewers score clarity as well as depth. "I used the PLC's online view to see whether the controller saw the sensor; it didn't" is clear to anyone, and still invites a deeper follow-up.

interview.q: Tell me about a time you diagnosed a difficult equipment failure.
rubric: Brief, clear Situation and Task (under about 30 seconds) with the impact of the failure stated
At least three distinct diagnostic steps, each with a reason, including at least one real measurement or data source and what it ruled out
Identifies a root cause (not only the part that was replaced) and explains how the fix was verified
Result is concrete and honest, ideally quantified (downtime, recurrence, cost), with a prevention or follow-up step
Clear about own role vs others, no blame, and ends with a lesson or a bridge to robotics or embedded debugging

interview.q: Describe a problem where your first hypothesis was wrong. How did you realize it, and what did you do next?
rubric: States the initial hypothesis and why it was reasonable at the time
Describes the specific test or observation that disproved it
Shows how the new evidence changed the next step (narrowing the problem, not restarting at random)
Reaches a verified root cause and a concrete result
Reflects honestly on what they'd do differently, without defensiveness

interview.q: Walk me through how you troubleshoot a system you've never seen before.
rubric: Starts with safety and with gathering information: symptoms, when it happens, recent changes, documentation, logs
Describes a systematic method, such as splitting the system in half or working from power to signal to logic, rather than guessing
Mentions measuring before replacing parts, and changing one thing at a time
Mentions verifying the fix under the conditions that caused the failure, and documenting it
Backs the method with a short real example and connects it to robotics or embedded systems
